plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) for obstructive sleep apnea: what the US-approved use covers, what AHI (the apnea-hypopnea index) measures, what the two SURMOUNT-OSA randomized trials showed at 52 weeks (one in people not using PAP, one in people using PAP), why weight is linked to sleep apnea, and questions to ask your doctor or sleep clinician
plan.angle: Same evergreen label-and-trial explainer, with these changes: (a) Thumbnail: 'SLEEP APNEA + TIRZEPATIDE' with subtext 'Fewer breathing pauses? Zepbound trials' (or 'FEWER BREATHING PAUSES?' with 'tirzepatide (Zepbound)' as subtext). One calm, fully drawn, labelled character in bed with a pen, no body imagery, and no snoring promise. (b) Title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound) for Sleep Apnea: What the Trials Showed'. (c) GI line, exactly as the label puts it: 'Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation are common. In the trials, the majority of nausea, vomiting and diarrhea events happened during dose escalation and decreased over time.' Don't use 'mostly'. (d) Give AHI results as events per hour per arm, with group sizes, the population and the measure, for each trial separately. Secondary outcomes only as printed in the paper, with both arms. (e) Keep everything else in the brief: the CPAP don't-stop line, the low-blood-sugar caveat for people on insulin or a sulfonylurea, the emergency card for severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting ('right away'), the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice', and the full 'Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you' line, all spoken and shown on screen.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) Sleep Apnea: What Trials Show
plan.why: A broad, approved-use question people search for, backed by settled primary sources (the US label and SURMOUNT-OSA in NEJM). It fills the beyond-weight gap and replaces the dropped Foundayo video without repeating today's Shorts. | fact-check: The topic is sound and in scope. In December 2024 the FDA approved tirzepatide (Zepbound) for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity, and SURMOUNT-OSA (Malhotra et al., NEJM 2024; two 52-week randomized trials, one without PAP and one with PAP) is a strong primary source. There is real search demand for this and it stays useful for months. It fits the 'Benefits beyond weight' pillar. The safety rules in the brief (CPAP don't-stop line, low blood sugar with insulin or a sulfonylurea, tirzepatide pancreatitis wording, no dosing or switching) are correct. Three things need fixing before scripting. (1) The thumbnail 'SNORING LESS?' promises something the video can't back up. The trials' main measure was AHI (breathing pauses or shallow breaths per hour), and snoring wasn't a reported endpoint, so the title and thumbnail would oversell. (2) The GI line in the brief, 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time', isn't the label's wording. The Zepbound PI says 'The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time', and our craft rules ban adding 'mostly'. Copy the label sentence. (3) Chapter 4 secondary results must come only from the NEJM paper or PubMed record, with both arms (for example the sleep-impairment and sleep-disturbance scores, oxygen-drop measures, blood pressure), and no causal 'because of weight loss' wording unless the paper says it. Keep every AHI figure in events per hour, with each trial's population (adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and obesity, without diabetes; no PAP vs using PAP) and the right measure ('counting everyone who started' vs 'if everyone stayed on treatment'). Don't compare the two trials as if they were head-to-head. Quote Section 1 from the 28 Aug 2026 PI word for word. Open with a sentence 1 that asks the question, without a 'Short answer.' label.

package.description:
Severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting? Call your healthcare provider right away. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Using CPAP or another positive airway pressure device? Don't stop or change it on your own. Talk to your sleep clinician first.

Quick answer: In two 52-week, double-blind randomized trials (SURMOUNT-OSA) in adults with moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea and obesity, without diabetes, the average apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) fell more on tirzepatide (Zepbound) than on placebo.
Trial 1, 234 adults not using PAP: −25.3 vs −5.3 events per hour.
Trial 2, 235 adults using PAP (measured after a 7-day PAP pause): −29.3 vs −5.5 events per hour.
The trials enrolled different people, so they aren't head-to-head. Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation are common. Low blood sugar is more likely with insulin or a sulfonylurea, and is also reported in adults without type 2 diabetes.

Sources:
Malhotra A, et al. N Engl J Med 2024: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38912654/
Zepbound US Prescribing Information (revised 28 Aug 2026): https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf

Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Trial 2 (235 adults using PAP, measured after a 7-day PAP pause) saw −29.3 vs −5.5. They enrolled different people, so it's not a head-to-head. Using CPAP? Don't stop or change it on your own. Talk to your sleep clinician first. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The script passes. I found four minor on-screen wording fixes, listed below, and nothing that needs a human.

**SURMOUNT-OSA (full text on PMC)**
- Trial sizes match: 234 in Trial 1 and 235 in Trial 2.
- Entry rules match: AHI of 15 or more events an hour, obesity, and anyone with type 1 or type 2 diabetes excluded.
- Both trials were double-blind and ran 52 weeks.
- The numbers count everyone who started (the "treatment-regimen" method).
- Starting AHI was 51.5 in Trial 1 and 49.5 in Trial 2, so "around fifty" is right.
- Trial 1: −25.3 vs −5.3 events an hour, difference −20.0, p<0.001.
- Trial 2: −29.3 vs −5.5, difference −23.8, p<0.001.
- The 7-day PAP pause before each sleep study in Trial 2 is quoted word for word in the paper, so the s43 loop payoff is accurate.
- Weight, systolic blood pressure, hypoxic burden, the inflammation marker (hsCRP) and the sleep questionnaires all improved significantly in both trials.

**Peppard, JAMA 2000**
- 690 Wisconsin adults, measured 4 years apart.
- A 10% weight gain went with about a 32% rise in AHI; a 10% loss went with about a 26% drop.
- The script correctly calls this a link, not proof.

**Schwartz, Proc Am Thorac Soc 2008**
- It supports the neck-fat and lung-volume ("loss of caudal traction") explanations and the collapsible airway. The script hedges these properly.

**Framing and safety**
- The script never treats the two trials as head-to-head (s44).
- The 175- and 350-a-night figures are labelled as our own arithmetic.
- The "Dan" story is clearly hypothetical.
- The safety lines are all there: don't stop PAP, the pancreatitis sign in tirzepatide's wording, the scoped don't-stop line, the low blood sugar caveat with "adults without type 2 diabetes", the boxed thyroid warning (MTC or MEN 2), and the disclaimer.

**Not checked**
- The Lilly PDF (S2) is live and downloaded, but its text wouldn't extract. That means I couldn't re-read the s06, s53, s55 or s56 wording against it. Those lines match the standing label notes and known Zepbound PI wording.
- PubMed pages wouldn't open (cookie wall). I confirmed the PubMed record URLs another way: S3's came up in search, and S1 and S4 point to the same papers I read in PMC full text.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three keep the outcome hidden (no hard-cap violations on giving the answer). #0 ('FEWER BREATHING PAUSES?') pairs a concrete, felt symptom with a visible question mark and a smiling-but-curious face that doesn't clash with the question tone; subtext clearly names tirzepatide (Zepbound), satisfying the drug-naming rule. It has the strongest single focal point (face + headline) and the clearest curiosity gap tied directly to the title's 'does it work?' promise. #1 ('2 TRIALS') is credible and legible but less emotionally gripping — a bare number is a weaker hook than a specific symptom question, and the moon-character focal point is less relatable than a human face. #2 ('SAME RESULT?') has a nice split-comparison layout but fails the house rule to name the drug in the thumbnail subtext (only CPAP status is labeled, no mention of tirzepatide/Zepbound), which is a concrete packaging defect per the craft notes. All three are legible at phone size with no cut-off text. Best pick: #0 for highest combined CTR and full compliance.
